I did a research paper in high school on the whole dispute. What's so funny to this day, is that if you asked people in 1989 on the likelihood of East Germany reunifying with the West vs. the islands being transferred to Japan, people would have sworn the latter would occur first and yet, it's been 27 years since the collapse of the Berlin Wall. 

Going back on-topic, the reason why Japan wants a formal peace treaty with Russia to end World War II, is due to an agreement both countries made in 1956. The [1956 Soviet-Japanese Joint Declaration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuril_Islands_dispute#1956_Soviet-Japanese_Joint_Declaration) states that if a peace treaty were to be signed, Iturup and Kunashiri will remain under Russian sovereignty while Shikotan and Habomai will be under Japanese control. So in essence, the framework of splitting the 4 disputed islands is already in place. However, there have been a couple of factors on both sides of why the dispute is still a big problem.

Reasons why Japan did not/couldn't accept the 1956 joint agreement:

* By accepting a peace treaty, Japan will automatically lose any future claim to Iturup and Kunashiri.
* The US intervened in the original deal, stating that if Japan concedes to giving up the islands then it should lay claim to Okinawa, which was already occupied at the time by the US.
* The US foreign policy at the time was a policy of containment against the threat of Communism, and any resolution of conflict between Japan and the USSR would be detrimental to that policy. Japan was seen as a bulwark against Communism as shown by the number of military bases and operations originating from Japan.
* The dispute to some Japanese nationalists has been ongoing fuel for claiming the victimization of Japan during WWII, being stabbed in the back by the breach of the Soviet-Japanese Neutrality pact, the seizure of the islands after August 15th 1945, and Japanese POWs that were left behind in the Soviet Union.
* The ongoing dispute solidifies the need for a US presence, due to a on-going threat of Soviet aggression.

Reasons why the Soviet Union did not/couldn't accept the 1956 joint agreement:

* The oceans around the islands are a strategic resource to Russia, with it separating the Sea of Okhotsk from the Pacific Ocean. During the Cold War, nuclear subs were stationed there to launch potential warheads against the US.
* The ocean is rich in marine life, due to the islands being in a location where cold and warm currents meet.
* If Russia were to lose territories occupied at the end of WWII, the US should also lose its claim of occupying Okinawa.
* If Russia "gives back" territories to Japan, there could be a wave of demands from Eastern Bloc countries.
* Over 2 generations of Russians lived and died on the islands, with many buried on its soil.
* The islands are a matter of national pride and winning the war on the eastern front.
* There was still some distrust of the Japanese, with Stalin in WWII comparing the surprise attack on Port Arthur in 1904 to that of 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor.

> doubt bioplastic is going to pass for some uses like say medical IV bags and surgical tubing

I work in medical device R&D and you'll probably not like what I am going to say. 

Polycarbonate fittings, which are commonly used in surgery contain BPA. There is physically no other means of synthesizing polycarbonate except for polymerizing BPA. So, unless you ban polycarbonate and significantly reduce the surgical suite to use glass and metal fittings that can withstand high pressures, they'll not going away. Even if it is against European REACH regulations.

Blood bags and surgical tubing is the opposite extreme. Both usually are made using plasticized (containing DEHP) PVC and there are other inferior alternatives (laminated LDPE, EVA, etc.) and more expensive alternatives (TPU) that cannot truly replicate the gas and water permeability of PVC. Turns out, the DEHP actually helps store the blood longer so the European Pharmacopoeia actually recommends the use of plasticized PVC for blood bags.

>From my experience in America and what I have seen online, the standard wait is 2 weeks (14 days) if they are interested in you.

Although I've applied to Japanese companies in the past, I've never accepted any jobs and I've only been working in the US all my life. However, here are some thoughts.

First off, we are in June now and no company in the world (that is not a relative of yours) can give you with 100% certainty that there is a job in December. The hiring of prospective entry level positions are the first positions on the chopping block when a company is going through financial difficulty, restructuring, or downsizing. I honestly wouldn't be surprised if your CEO tells you in November "sorry bud, company is going through bad times" when he already knew that he will need to twist multiple arms to seriously hire you off-cycle.  

Second, as other mentioned the hiring process usually is in April of each year and Japanese companies usually do not do mid-year hires. If it is necessary, it would be a special case and you can expect an extra layer of bureaucracy if they are seriously interested in you. This is on top of usually a (1) Physical resume drop-off at a booth at a conference/event, (2) Surviving the in-person interview panel, and (3) Waiting for the on-site interview (aka "Final Interview" 最終面接) where you actually meet your hiring manger and their boss.  It sounds you only finished Step 1, so if you don't hear anything back soon then you are either rejected or in the backup pile.

Lastly, a 2 week wait from my perspective is usually the tail-end of when a US company should have already made a decision on you or if they are just about to schedule a phone interview. Most online applications I made provide e-mail responses within 2-8 days, and this is knowing in advance that I am within the top 10% of the application pool. If it takes more than 2 weeks, it usually means: (1) There are way too many applicants and you might not get your turn or pending, (2) Your resume/application was filtered out, (3) Your application is not competitive and in the backup pile. 

Since you are in a special situation where you are waiting for a job in 6 months and would be a referral by your CEO, you will probably need to patient. However, an inquiry every 2 weeks would probably not hurt to keep them aware that you haven't dropped your interest/application.
